fatal_errors: The proposed initially single-phase B2/BCC alloy does not match the as-cast FCC+B2 AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA.

The hypothesis attributes embrittlement to grain-boundary precipitates and reduced grain-boundary cohesion, whereas the target mechanism involves enhanced L12 ordering, restricted cross-slip and planar slip, and stress concentration at jagged FCC/B2 phase-boundary tips.
It omits the decisive non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile response, including maximum embrittlement near 600 degrees C and ductility recovery near 750 degrees C.
No defined 550-750 degrees C aging window or comparison across multiple aging temperatures is proposed.
Thermal aging and cyclic loading are varied together, preventing attribution of any observed degradation to aging-induced structural evolution.
The cited evidence supports precipitation strengthening or B2/BCC decomposition in other HEAs but does not support grain-boundary precipitation-driven toughness loss under cyclic loading.
explanation: The answer addresses the broad possibility of service-induced HEA embrittlement and proposes measurable mechanical and microscopy outcomes, but it largely reinstates a conventional grain-boundary precipitation mechanism rather than distinguishing the relevant phase-boundary and ordering mechanism. Its experiment compares only an untreated state with a combined aging-plus-cycling treatment, lacks temperature-resolved controls, and cannot reveal the target ductile-brittle-ductile transition. A discriminating test would age the same FCC+B2 alloy below 550 degrees C, near 600 degrees C, and near 750 degrees C, then correlate ductility with L12 order, antiphase-boundary energy or planar slip, jagged phase-boundary density, dislocation pile-ups, and crack initiation at phase-boundary tips while excluding impurity segregation. The proposed falsification rule is also weak because it requires both no embrittlement and no precipitates; precipitates without embrittlement or embrittlement without precipitates would be more informative causal tests.
